intro: Before you rises the Sultan Ahmed Mosque, a mosque and complex in İstanbul province, built in 1609–1617. Count its six minarets, then step inside to meet the twenty thousand İznik tiles that line its walls. It was raised directly opposite Hagia Sophia, over the old Byzantine palace.
history: Ahmed I was just nineteen when he chose his site: the ruins of the Byzantine Great Palace, facing Hagia Sophia. He became the first sultan to raise such a mosque without the spoils of a victory to pay for it. Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa completed the work between 1609 and 1617. And those six minarets? They were read as a claim to equal the sanctuary at Mecca, so a seventh was added there.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the main dome and its semi-domes, the six minarets and the İznik tiles. Look out for the Imperial Lodge, visit the Tomb of Ahmed I, and finish in the courtyard with its fountain.
facts: Did you know? The tiles that give it the name 'Blue Mosque' came from İznik, and the order was so large that it drove the workshops' prices past recovery — İznik tilemaking never regained its footing. At the time, six minarets were matched only by the sanctuary at Mecca; when the claim caused offence, a further minaret was added there. The mosque is still a place of prayer, so visiting hours shift with the prayer times, and there is no entry charge. And beneath it lies the Byzantine Great Palace, whose mosaic floor still rests in place in the museum behind the mosque.
outro: This brings our journey through the Sultan Ahmed Mosque to an end. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. These stones have waited for centuries; let them keep waiting for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
